title: The wrongdoer wrongs himself
hook: whoever does wrong, wrongs himself first (Meditations 9.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was cutting teeth: Marcus sets dying among nature's ordinary works. Your line was nature's work.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, then makes a rude gesture for good measure. In the moment there's only one victim, and it's you. But follow that driver home. The rest of their evening is still inside that anger. Their shoulders are still up; their day is still a little worse for it. Marcus wrote a very short entry in book nine about exactly this, two lines long.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `FOLLOW THEM HOME.` → `THE WRONGDOER WRONGS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: In George Long's 1862 translation: “He who does wrong does wrong against himself.” Then Marcus adds: whoever acts unjustly acts unjustly toward himself, because he makes himself bad. For Marcus, the only real harm is harm to your character, the ruling part of you. Your car, your schedule, even your body can be damaged by someone else. Your goodness can be damaged only by you. So the person who wrongs you has, at most, dented your fender. They've dented their own self. If that's true, the wrongdoer isn't someone to hate. They're someone to pity, the way you'd pity a person who stepped on their own foot and then blamed the floor. That isn't looking down on them. It's seeing the injury clearly. The very next entry keeps this honest: a person can act unjustly by not doing something, too. So pity is no reason to stand by; standing by can be a wrong of its own. What shifts is the feeling underneath. Not, how dare they, but what did that cost them? And by Marcus's logic it cuts close to home: every time we snap, cheat, or lie, the first person changed is the one who did it.
screen: `WRONG DONE IS WRONG TO ONESELF.` · `ONLY YOU CAN DAMAGE YOUR GOODNESS.` · `PITY, NOT HATE.` · `NOT DOING CAN BE UNJUST, TOO.` · then, large: `HE'S HURT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who wronged you, a small or middle-sized wrong, not your deepest wound. Picture them afterward: the evening that followed, what they had to tell themselves, what kind of person that act made them a little more of. See if a sliver of pity shows up beside the anger; it doesn't excuse them, it just sees them.
George Long, whose translation gives Marcus's short entry: he who does wrong does wrong against himself, and makes himself worse. Today's word.
Your line: he's hurt himself. Pity sees the injury without excusing it. Day six hundred eight, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this line to turn anger toward someone who wronged them into something closer to pity, while still acting to protect themselves and others.

original.note: Greek: to do wrong, to err. Marcus's line turns on this verb.

trapdoor: what you thought: what goes around comes around.
what it means: there's no waiting for payback; the wrong itself makes the wrongdoer worse, right away.
what a scholar hears: Marcus echoes an old Socratic claim, argued in Plato's Gorgias, that doing injustice is worse for the doer than suffering it.
recall: Latin for delay, a cure for anger

notes: Confirm Long's wording of 9.4: 'He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.'
9.5 (Long): 'He often acts unjustly who does not do a certain thing; not only he who does a certain thing.' Paraphrased; confirm.
Original: confirm that 9.4 uses ἁμαρτάνων (Ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ἑαυτῷ ἁμαρτάνει).
Gorgias reference for 'doing injustice is worse than suffering it': confirm Stephanus numbers.
